key.entities.key.doc.full_as_xml: <Class file="/Users/appthreat/sandbox/swift4415/argparser-demo/.build/checkouts/Yams/Sources/Yams/AliasDereferencingStrategy.swift" line="20" column="17"><Name>AliasDereferencingStrategy</Name><USR>s:4Yams26AliasDereferencingStrategyP</USR><Declaration>protocol AliasDereferencingStrategy : AnyObject</Declaration><CommentParts><Abstract><Para>A class-bound protocol which implements a strategy for dereferencing aliases (or dealiasing) values during YAML document decoding. YAML documents which do not contain anchors will not benefit from the use of an AliasDereferencingStrategy in any way. The main use-case for dereferencing aliases in a YML document is when decoding into class types. If the yaml document is large and contains many references (perhaps it is a representation of a dense graph) then, decoding into structs will require the of large amounts of system memory to represent highly redundant (duplicated) data structures. However, if the same document is decoded into class types and the decoding uses an <codeVoice>AliasDereferencingStrategy</codeVoice> such as <codeVoice>BasicAliasDereferencingStrategy</codeVoice> then the emitted value will have its class references coalesced. No duplicate objects will be initialized (unless identical objects have multiple distinct anchors in the YAML document). In some scenarios this may significantly reduce the memory footprint of the decoded type.</Para></Abstract></CommentParts></Class>

This operation isn’t guaranteed to be stable, so the relative ordering of elements within the partitions might change.</Para><Para>In the following example, an array of numbers is partitioned by a predicate that matches elements greater than 30.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[var numbers = [30, 40, 20, 30, 30, 60, 10]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let p = numbers.partition(by: { $0 > 30 })]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// p == 5]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// numbers == [30, 10, 20, 30, 30, 60, 40]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>The <codeVoice>numbers</codeVoice> array is now arranged in two partitions. If the collection doesn’t support an internal representation in a form of contiguous storage, the method doesn’t call <codeVoice>body</codeVoice> — it immediately returns <codeVoice>nil</codeVoice>.</Para><Para>The optimizer can often eliminate bounds- and uniqueness-checking within an algorithm. These counters can be used as indices only in instances of zero-based, integer-indexed collections, such as <codeVoice>Array</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>ContiguousArray</codeVoice>. For other collections the counters may be out of range or of the wrong type to use as an index. To iterate over the elements of a collection with its indices, use the <codeVoice>zip(_:_:)</codeVoice> function.</Para><Para>This example iterates over the indices and elements of a set, building a list consisting of indices of names with five or fewer letters.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let names: Set = ["Sofia", "Camilla", "Martina", "Mateo", "Nicolás"]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[var shorterIndices: [Set<String>.Index] = []]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[for (i, name) in zip(names.indices, names) {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    if name.count <= 5 {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[        shorterIndices.append(i)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    }]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>Now that the <codeVoice>shorterIndices</codeVoice> array holds the indices of the shorter names in the <codeVoice>names</codeVoice> set, you can use those indices to access elements in the set.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[for i in shorterIndices {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    print(names[i])]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "Sofia"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "Mateo"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Complexity><Para>O(1)</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

If the sequence has no elements, returns <codeVoice>nil</codeVoice>.</Para></ResultDiscussion><Discussion><Para>The predicate must be a <emphasis>strict weak ordering</emphasis> over the elements. That is, for any elements <codeVoice>a</codeVoice>, <codeVoice>b</codeVoice>, and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice>, the following conditions must hold:</Para><List-Bullet><Item><Para><codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, a)</codeVoice> is always <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>. (Irreflexivity)</Para></Item><Item><Para>If <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, b)</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(b, c)</codeVoice> are both <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>, then <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, c)</codeVoice> is also <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>. (Transitive comparability)</Para></Item><Item><Para>Two elements are <emphasis>incomparable</emphasis> if neither is ordered before the other according to the predicate. If <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> are incomparable, and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are incomparable, then <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are also incomparable. (Transitive incomparability)</Para></Item></List-Bullet><Para>This example shows how to use the <codeVoice>min(by:)</codeVoice> method on a dictionary to find the key-value pair with the lowest value.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let hues = ["Heliotrope": 296, "Coral": 16, "Aquamarine": 156]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let leastHue = hues.min { a, b in a.value < b.value }]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(leastHue)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "Optional((key: "Coral", value: 16))"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Complexity><Para>O(<emphasis>n</emphasis>), where <emphasis>n</emphasis> is the length of the sequence.</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

This example shows how to build a dictionary of letter frequencies of a string.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let letters = "abracadabra"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let letterCount = letters.reduce(into: [:]) { counts, letter in]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    counts[letter, default: 0] += 1]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// letterCount == ["a": 5, "b": 2, "r": 2, "c": 1, "d": 1]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>When <codeVoice>letters.reduce(into:_:)</codeVoice> is called, the following steps occur:</Para><List-Number><Item><Para>The <codeVoice>updateAccumulatingResult</codeVoice> closure is called with the initial accumulating value—<codeVoice>[:]</codeVoice> in this case—and the first character of <codeVoice>letters</codeVoice>, modifying the accumulating value by setting <codeVoice>1</codeVoice> for the key <codeVoice>"a"</codeVoice>.</Para></Item><Item><Para>The closure is called again repeatedly with the updated accumulating value and each element of the sequence.</Para></Item><Item><Para>When the sequence is exhausted, the accumulating value is returned to the caller.</Para></Item></List-Number><Para>If the sequence has no elements, <codeVoice>updateAccumulatingResult</codeVoice> is never executed and <codeVoice>initialResult</codeVoice> is the result of the call to <codeVoice>reduce(into:_:)</codeVoice>.</Para><Complexity><Para>O(<emphasis>n</emphasis>), where <emphasis>n</emphasis> is the length of the sequence.</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

The elements of the resulting array are ordered according to the given predicate.</Para><Para>In the following example, the predicate provides an ordering for an array of a custom <codeVoice>HTTPResponse</codeVoice> type. The predicate orders errors before successes and sorts the error responses by their error code.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[enum HTTPResponse {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case ok]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case error(Int)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let responses: [HTTPResponse] = [.error(500), .ok, .ok, .error(404), .error(403)]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let sortedResponses = responses.sorted {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    switch ($0, $1) {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // Order errors by code]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case let (.error(aCode), .error(bCode)):]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[        return aCode < bCode]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // All successes are equivalent, so none is before any other]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.ok, .ok): return false]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // Order errors before successes]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.error, .ok): return true]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.ok, .error): return false]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    }]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(sortedResponses)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "[.error(403), .error(404), .error(500), .ok, .ok]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>You also use this method to sort elements that conform to the <codeVoice>Comparable</codeVoice> protocol in descending order. To sort your sequence in descending order, pass the greater-than operator (<codeVoice>></codeVoice>) as the <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder</codeVoice> parameter.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let students: Set = ["Kofi", "Abena", "Peter", "Kweku", "Akosua"]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let descendingStudents = students.sorted(by: >)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(descendingStudents)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Peter", "Kweku", "Kofi", "Akosua", "Abena"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>Calling the related <codeVoice>sorted()</codeVoice> method is equivalent to calling this method and passing the less-than operator (<codeVoice><</codeVoice>) as the predicate.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(students.sorted())]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Abena", "Akosua", "Kofi", "Kweku", "Peter"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(students.sorted(by: <))]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Abena", "Akosua", "Kofi", "Kweku", "Peter"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>The predicate must be a <emphasis>strict weak ordering</emphasis> over the elements. That is, for any elements <codeVoice>a</codeVoice>, <codeVoice>b</codeVoice>, and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice>, the following conditions must hold:</Para><List-Bullet><Item><Para><codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, a)</codeVoice> is always <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>. (Irreflexivity)</Para></Item><Item><Para>If <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, b)</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(b, c)</codeVoice> are both <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>, then <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, c)</codeVoice> is also <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>. (Transitive comparability)</Para></Item><Item><Para>Two elements are <emphasis>incomparable</emphasis> if neither is ordered before the other according to the predicate. If <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> are incomparable, and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are incomparable, then <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are also incomparable. (Transitive incomparability)</Para></Item></List-Bullet><Para>The sorting algorithm is guaranteed to be stable. A stable sort preserves the relative order of elements for which <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder</codeVoice> does not establish an order.</Para><Complexity><Para>O(<emphasis>n</emphasis> log <emphasis>n</emphasis>), where <emphasis>n</emphasis> is the length of the sequence.</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

key.entities.key.doc.full_as_xml: <Function><Name>sorted(by:)</Name><USR>s:STsE6sorted2bySay7ElementQzGSbAD_ADtKXE_tKF::SYNTHESIZED::s:4Yams4NodeO7MappingV</USR><Declaration>@inlinable func sorted(by areInIncreasingOrder: ((key: Yams.Node, value: Yams.Node), (key: Yams.Node, value: Yams.Node)) throws -> Bool) rethrows -> [(key: Yams.Node, value: Yams.Node)]</Declaration><CommentParts><Abstract><Para>Returns the elements of the sequence, sorted using the given predicate as the comparison between elements.</Para></Abstract><Parameters><Parameter><Name>areInIncreasingOrder</Name><Direction isExplicit="0">in</Direction><Discussion><Para>A predicate that returns <codeVoice>true</codeVoice> if its first argument should be ordered before its second argument; otherwise, <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>.</Para></Discussion></Parameter></Parameters><ResultDiscussion><Para>A sorted array of the sequence’s elements.</Para></ResultDiscussion><Discussion><Para>When you want to sort a sequence of elements that don’t conform to the <codeVoice>Comparable</codeVoice> protocol, pass a predicate to this method that returns <codeVoice>true</codeVoice> when the first element should be ordered before the second. The elements of the resulting array are ordered according to the given predicate.</Para><Para>In the following example, the predicate provides an ordering for an array of a custom <codeVoice>HTTPResponse</codeVoice> type. The predicate orders errors before successes and sorts the error responses by their error code.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[enum HTTPResponse {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case ok]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case error(Int)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let responses: [HTTPResponse] = [.error(500), .ok, .ok, .error(404), .error(403)]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let sortedResponses = responses.sorted {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    switch ($0, $1) {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // Order errors by code]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case let (.error(aCode), .error(bCode)):]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[        return aCode < bCode]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // All successes are equivalent, so none is before any other]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.ok, .ok): return false]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // Order errors before successes]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.error, .ok): return true]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.ok, .error): return false]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    }]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(sortedResponses)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "[.error(403), .error(404), .error(500), .ok, .ok]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>You also use this method to sort elements that conform to the <codeVoice>Comparable</codeVoice> protocol in descending order. To sort your sequence in descending order, pass the greater-than operator (<codeVoice>></codeVoice>) as the <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder</codeVoice> parameter.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let students: Set = ["Kofi", "Abena", "Peter", "Kweku", "Akosua"]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let descendingStudents = students.sorted(by: >)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(descendingStudents)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Peter", "Kweku", "Kofi", "Akosua", "Abena"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>Calling the related <codeVoice>sorted()</codeVoice> method is equivalent to calling this method and passing the less-than operator (<codeVoice><</codeVoice>) as the predicate.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(students.sorted())]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Abena", "Akosua", "Kofi", "Kweku", "Peter"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(students.sorted(by: <))]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Abena", "Akosua", "Kofi", "Kweku", "Peter"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>The predicate must be a <emphasis>strict weak ordering</emphasis> over the elements. That is, for any elements <codeVoice>a</codeVoice>, <codeVoice>b</codeVoice>, and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice>, the following conditions must hold:</Para><List-Bullet><Item><Para><codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, a)</codeVoice> is always <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>. (Irreflexivity)</Para></Item><Item><Para>If <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, b)</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(b, c)</codeVoice> are both <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>, then <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, c)</codeVoice> is also <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>. (Transitive comparability)</Para></Item><Item><Para>Two elements are <emphasis>incomparable</emphasis> if neither is ordered before the other according to the predicate. If <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> are incomparable, and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are incomparable, then <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are also incomparable. (Transitive incomparability)</Para></Item></List-Bullet><Para>The sorting algorithm is guaranteed to be stable. A stable sort preserves the relative order of elements for which <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder</codeVoice> does not establish an order.</Para><Complexity><Para>O(<emphasis>n</emphasis> log <emphasis>n</emphasis>), where <emphasis>n</emphasis> is the length of the sequence.</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

Implementations should return RedundancyAliasingOutcome.anchor(…) for the first occurrence of a value. Subsequent occurrences of the same value (where same-ness is defined by the implementation) should return RedundancyAliasingOutcome.alias(…) where the contained Anchor has the same value as the previously returned RedundancyAliasingOutcome.anchor(…). Its the identity of the Anchor values returned that ultimately informs the YAML encoder when to use aliases. N,B. It is essential that implementations release all references to Anchors which are created by this type when releaseAnchorReferences() is called by the Encoder. After this call the implementation will no longer be referenced by the Encoder and will itself be released.</Para></Abstract></CommentParts></Class>

If the contiguous storage doesn’t exist, the collection creates it. If the collection doesn’t support an internal representation in a form of contiguous storage, the method doesn’t call <codeVoice>body</codeVoice> — it immediately returns <codeVoice>nil</codeVoice>.</Para><Para>The optimizer can often eliminate bounds- and uniqueness-checking within an algorithm. When that fails, however, invoking the same algorithm on the <codeVoice>buffer</codeVoice> argument may let you trade safety for speed.</Para><Para>Successive calls to this method may provide a different pointer on each call. Don’t store <codeVoice>buffer</codeVoice> outside of this method.</Para><Para>A <codeVoice>Collection</codeVoice> that provides its own implementation of this method must provide contiguous storage to its elements in the same order as they appear in the collection. This guarantees that it’s possible to generate contiguous mutable storage to any of its subsequences by slicing <codeVoice>buffer</codeVoice> with a range formed from the distances to the subsequence’s <codeVoice>startIndex</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>endIndex</codeVoice>, respectively.</Para><Note><Para>This documentation comment was inherited from <codeVoice>Sequence</codeVoice>.</Para></Note></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

key.entities.key.doc.full_as_xml: <Function><Name>enumerated()</Name><USR>s:STsE10enumerateds18EnumeratedSequenceVyxGyF::SYNTHESIZED::s:4Yams12YamlSequenceV</USR><Declaration>@inlinable func enumerated() -> EnumeratedSequence<Yams.YamlSequence<T>></Declaration><CommentParts><Abstract><Para>Returns a sequence of pairs (<emphasis>n</emphasis>, <emphasis>x</emphasis>), where <emphasis>n</emphasis> represents a consecutive integer starting at zero and <emphasis>x</emphasis> represents an element of the sequence.</Para></Abstract><ResultDiscussion><Para>A sequence of pairs enumerating the sequence.</Para></ResultDiscussion><Discussion><Para>This example enumerates the characters of the string “Swift” and prints each character along with its place in the string.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[for (n, c) in "Swift".enumerated() {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    print("\(n): '\(c)'")]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "0: 'S'"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "1: 'w'"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "2: 'i'"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "3: 'f'"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "4: 't'"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>When you enumerate a collection, the integer part of each pair is a counter for the enumeration, but is not necessarily the index of the paired value. These counters can be used as indices only in instances of zero-based, integer-indexed collections, such as <codeVoice>Array</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>ContiguousArray</codeVoice>. For other collections the counters may be out of range or of the wrong type to use as an index. To iterate over the elements of a collection with its indices, use the <codeVoice>zip(_:_:)</codeVoice> function.</Para><Para>This example iterates over the indices and elements of a set, building a list consisting of indices of names with five or fewer letters.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let names: Set = ["Sofia", "Camilla", "Martina", "Mateo", "Nicolás"]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[var shorterIndices: [Set<String>.Index] = []]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[for (i, name) in zip(names.indices, names) {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    if name.count <= 5 {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[        shorterIndices.append(i)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    }]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>Now that the <codeVoice>shorterIndices</codeVoice> array holds the indices of the shorter names in the <codeVoice>names</codeVoice> set, you can use those indices to access elements in the set.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[for i in shorterIndices {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    print(names[i])]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "Sofia"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "Mateo"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Complexity><Para>O(1)</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

key.entities.key.doc.full_as_xml: <Function><Name>sorted(by:)</Name><USR>s:STsE6sorted2bySay7ElementQzGSbAD_ADtKXE_tKF::SYNTHESIZED::s:4Yams12YamlSequenceV</USR><Declaration>@inlinable func sorted(by areInIncreasingOrder: (T, T) throws -> Bool) rethrows -> [T]</Declaration><CommentParts><Abstract><Para>Returns the elements of the sequence, sorted using the given predicate as the comparison between elements.</Para></Abstract><Parameters><Parameter><Name>areInIncreasingOrder</Name><Direction isExplicit="0">in</Direction><Discussion><Para>A predicate that returns <codeVoice>true</codeVoice> if its first argument should be ordered before its second argument; otherwise, <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>.</Para></Discussion></Parameter></Parameters><ResultDiscussion><Para>A sorted array of the sequence’s elements.</Para></ResultDiscussion><Discussion><Para>When you want to sort a sequence of elements that don’t conform to the <codeVoice>Comparable</codeVoice> protocol, pass a predicate to this method that returns <codeVoice>true</codeVoice> when the first element should be ordered before the second. The elements of the resulting array are ordered according to the given predicate.</Para><Para>In the following example, the predicate provides an ordering for an array of a custom <codeVoice>HTTPResponse</codeVoice> type. The predicate orders errors before successes and sorts the error responses by their error code.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[enum HTTPResponse {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case ok]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case error(Int)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let responses: [HTTPResponse] = [.error(500), .ok, .ok, .error(404), .error(403)]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let sortedResponses = responses.sorted {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    switch ($0, $1) {]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // Order errors by code]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case let (.error(aCode), .error(bCode)):]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[        return aCode < bCode]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // All successes are equivalent, so none is before any other]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.ok, .ok): return false]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    // Order errors before successes]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.error, .ok): return true]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    case (.ok, .error): return false]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[    }]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[}]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(sortedResponses)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "[.error(403), .error(404), .error(500), .ok, .ok]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>You also use this method to sort elements that conform to the <codeVoice>Comparable</codeVoice> protocol in descending order. To sort your sequence in descending order, pass the greater-than operator (<codeVoice>></codeVoice>) as the <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder</codeVoice> parameter.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let students: Set = ["Kofi", "Abena", "Peter", "Kweku", "Akosua"]]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let descendingStudents = students.sorted(by: >)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(descendingStudents)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Peter", "Kweku", "Kofi", "Akosua", "Abena"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>Calling the related <codeVoice>sorted()</codeVoice> method is equivalent to calling this method and passing the less-than operator (<codeVoice><</codeVoice>) as the predicate.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(students.sorted())]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Abena", "Akosua", "Kofi", "Kweku", "Peter"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(students.sorted(by: <))]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["Abena", "Akosua", "Kofi", "Kweku", "Peter"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>The predicate must be a <emphasis>strict weak ordering</emphasis> over the elements. That is, for any elements <codeVoice>a</codeVoice>, <codeVoice>b</codeVoice>, and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice>, the following conditions must hold:</Para><List-Bullet><Item><Para><codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, a)</codeVoice> is always <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>. (Irreflexivity)</Para></Item><Item><Para>If <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, b)</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(b, c)</codeVoice> are both <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>, then <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder(a, c)</codeVoice> is also <codeVoice>true</codeVoice>. (Transitive comparability)</Para></Item><Item><Para>Two elements are <emphasis>incomparable</emphasis> if neither is ordered before the other according to the predicate. If <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> are incomparable, and <codeVoice>b</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are incomparable, then <codeVoice>a</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>c</codeVoice> are also incomparable. (Transitive incomparability)</Para></Item></List-Bullet><Para>The sorting algorithm is guaranteed to be stable. A stable sort preserves the relative order of elements for which <codeVoice>areInIncreasingOrder</codeVoice> does not establish an order.</Para><Complexity><Para>O(<emphasis>n</emphasis> log <emphasis>n</emphasis>), where <emphasis>n</emphasis> is the length of the sequence.</Para></Complexity></Discussion></CommentParts></Function>

The default value is <codeVoice>Int.max</codeVoice>.</Para></Discussion></Parameter><Parameter><Name>omittingEmptySubsequences</Name><Direction isExplicit="0">in</Direction><Discussion><Para>If <codeVoice>false</codeVoice>, an empty subsequence is returned in the result for each consecutive pair of <codeVoice>separator</codeVoice> elements in the sequence and for each instance of <codeVoice>separator</codeVoice> at the start or end of the sequence. Elements that are used to split the sequence are not returned as part of any subsequence.</Para><Para>The following examples show the effects of the <codeVoice>maxSplits</codeVoice> and <codeVoice>omittingEmptySubsequences</codeVoice> parameters when splitting a string at each space character (” “). The first use of <codeVoice>split</codeVoice> returns each word that was originally separated by one or more spaces.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[let line = "BLANCHE:   I don't want realism. I want magic!"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(line.split(separator: " ")]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[          .map(String.init))]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["BLANCHE:", "I", "don\'t", "want", "realism.", "I", "want", "magic!"]"]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered></zCodeLineNumbered></CodeListing><Para>The second example passes <codeVoice>1</codeVoice> for the <codeVoice>maxSplits</codeVoice> parameter, so the original string is split just once, into two new strings.</Para><CodeListing language="swift"><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[print(line.split(separator: " ", maxSplits: 1)]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[          .map(String.init))]]></zCodeLineNumbered><zCodeLineNumbered><![CDATA[// Prints "["BLANCHE:", "  I don\'t want realism.
